title: A Real Snowstorm Is Hitting Missouri on Thanksgiving Day — The Difference Between "Cold" and "Buried" for Balcony Containers
intro: NWS St. Louis put a Winter Storm Warning into effect at 1:03 a.m. CST today, running until 6:00 p.m. CST tomorrow — Thanksgiving Day itself. Local coverage from FOX2 St. Louis and KBSI Cape Girardeau has the heaviest band tracking through the eastern Ozarks toward Farmington, with FOX2 forecasting 3-6 inches and some spots over 6, and KBSI putting it at 4-7 inches likely with localized totals of 8-10+ inches. NWS Paducah has a separate Winter Weather Advisory out for Butler, Carter, Ripley, Scott, and Stoddard Counties in southeast Missouri (1-3 inches, 3 p.m. today to 3 p.m. tomorrow), while NWS Springfield expects the central Ozarks to see less, since warm ground and air temperatures through Thursday daytime should limit accumulation there. Snow starts tonight into tomorrow morning, then switches to cold rain north to south during the day. Every outlet flags the same caveat: this is a narrow band, and a small shift in the storm track changes the totals a lot from one town to the next. We've covered plenty of "it's going to be cold" posts this month. This one is different — it's actual accumulating, wet snow sitting on top of whatever is still on your balcony when you leave for the holiday.

sections.heading: Cold kills roots slowly; wet snow breaks things fast
sections.body: A hard freeze is a slow problem — it damages a plant over hours as cell water crystallizes. Several inches of wet snow sitting on a plant is a fast, mechanical problem: it just weighs the thing down until something gives. A trellis, a tomato cage, a leggy rosemary or a small citrus with a full canopy can snap a branch or tip a whole pot under a load that would be a non-event for a garden bed shrub rooted in the ground. In the KBSI and FOX2 coverage area (the band running toward Farmington, where the higher 4-10+ inch totals are forecast), that's enough wet snow to matter for anything top-heavy in a container. If you're leaving for Thanksgiving before this clears tonight or tomorrow morning, the move is to either lay anything with a full canopy on its side on the balcony floor (lower profile sheds less and can't tip) or bring it just inside the door, rather than leaving it standing upright and loaded.

products.name: Reusable frost blanket / floating row cover
products.blurb: A lightweight fabric cover doesn't stop snow from landing, but it keeps several inches of it from sitting directly against foliage and stems, and it sheds more easily than bare leaves do when you knock it off after the storm clears.
products.priceNote: A single reusable cover is inexpensive and gets reused for every freeze or snow event the rest of the season.

sections.heading: The snow-to-rain switch is the part that actually threatens terracotta
sections.body: Every forecast in this storm has the same shape: snow first, then a changeover to cold rain as temperatures climb through Thanksgiving Day. That transition is worse for unglazed clay pots than the snow itself. Snowmelt and rain soak into a porous terracotta wall, and if temperatures drop back below freezing afterward (which is realistic once the rain clears out behind the system), that trapped moisture expands and can crack or spall the pot — the same freeze-thaw cycle that ruins driveways and sidewalks, just happening to your planter instead. If you've got terracotta or ceramic containers in or near the path of this system, wrapping them now, before the first snow falls tonight, matters more than anything you'd do after the rain starts.

products.name: Burlap pot insulation wrap
products.blurb: Wrapping a terracotta or ceramic pot in burlap before a snow-to-rain cycle slows how much moisture the clay wall actually absorbs, which is what prevents the freeze-thaw cracking this kind of storm sets up.
products.priceNote: Sold by the roll and reusable across multiple pots and storms.
products.searchQuery: burlap pot insulation wrap winter protection

sections.heading: If you're traveling through or leaving from this band, don't wait on the forecast to change your mind
sections.body: Every local source is explicit that the heaviest-snow line is narrow and could shift onto or off of any specific town between now and tomorrow morning. If you're packing to leave for Thanksgiving from anywhere in that St. Louis-to-Farmington corridor, or from the southeast Missouri counties under the Paducah advisory, the practical call is to bring container plants in before you leave rather than waiting for a forecast update that might arrive after you're already gone. For anything too heavy to carry easily — a large mixed planter, a dwarf citrus in a big pot — a wheeled plant caddy set underneath ahead of time turns a last-minute, five-minute decision into something you can actually do solo on your way out the door.

products.name: Wheeled plant caddy / rolling plant stand
products.blurb: Sliding a wheeled caddy under a heavy container ahead of the storm means moving it indoors or against a sheltered wall is a quick roll, not a two-person lift, which matters if you're trying to beat a storm on your way to the airport or the highway.
products.priceNote: A one-time purchase sized to your largest pot's base diameter and weight rating.

conclusion: None of this is the kind of forecast that makes national news — it's a regional Thanksgiving snow event that local Missouri and southern Illinois outlets are covering as a travel and roads story. But if you're an apartment or balcony grower anywhere in or near that band, it's a mechanically different threat than the cold-air stories we've covered this month: actual accumulating snow that can break or tip top-heavy containers, followed by a rain changeover that's specifically bad for unglazed clay pots. If you're in the affected corridor and leaving town today or tomorrow, the cheap insurance is the same either way — lay down or bring in anything top-heavy, wrap any terracotta you can't move, and don't bet on the narrow band missing your specific block.
